title: Quickstart
text:
Models by Use Case

I need protein sequence embeddings or representations
Recommended: ESMC - Latest foundation protein language model - Trained on diverse metagenomic protein sequences - Produces improved protein representations - Recommended for new projects
Alternative: ESM-2 (for legacy compatibility) - Proven and well documented - Extensively used in published research - Best choice when reproducing existing workflows


I want to design new proteins or generate sequences
Recommended: ESM3

Generates entirely new proteins
Supports chain-of-thought iterative refinement
Produces proteins far beyond natural sequence space
Excellent for:

Motif scaffolding
Functional protein design
Novel protein discovery


Alternative
If ESM3 isn’t appropriate, use:

ESMFold2 + ESMC for inverse protein design workflows.

title: Decision Tree
text:
1. What’s your primary goal?


A. I need protein sequence representations or embeddings
→ Go to Section 2A


B. I want to design or generate protein sequences
→ Go to Section 2B


C. I need to predict 3D protein structures
→ Go to Section 2C


D. I want to understand or score protein mutations
→ Go to Section 2D

title: Decision Tree
text:
2A. Sequence Representations & Embeddings

What’s your use case?
I’m doing research and want the best representations → Use ESMC (latest, best quality, metagenomic training) - Model Card - Tutorial: Getting Embeddings - GitHub
I have existing ESM2 code and want to upgrade → Use ESMC (drop-in replacement, but see migration guide) - Migration Guide - Comparison Table
I’m using legacy code tied to ESM2 → Stay with ESM2 (for now) - ESM2 Docs - Plan migration to ESMC when ready
I want to fine-tune on my own data → Use ESMC - Fine-tuning Tutorial - Larger models (6B) work best, but 300M is faster for experiments
I need this to be very fast → Use ESMC-300M - Smallest model, still high quality - Much faster inference than larger models

title: Decision Tree
text:
2B. Protein Design & Generation

What do you want to design?
De novo proteins (completely new sequences) → Use ESM3 - Model Card - Design Tutorial - Paper
Protein binders (antibodies, miniproteins) → Use ESM3 with ESMFold2 - Generate sequences with ESM3 - Validate structures with ESMFold2 - Binder Design Example
Enzyme variants (improving existing proteins) → Use ESMC + ESMFold2 - Score mutations with ESMC embeddings - Validate with structure prediction - Directed Evolution Example

title: Decision Tree
text:
2C. Structure Prediction

What type of structure do you need?
Single protein chain (monomers) → Use ESMFold2-Fast - Fastest option - Excellent accuracy - Tutorial
Protein complexes (antibody-antigen, PPIs, multimers) → Use ESMFold2 - State-of-the-art accuracy - Handles up to 768 residues (all chains combined) - Complex Prediction Tutorial
Large complexes (>768 residues) → Use ESMFold2-Fast on individual chains, then dock manually - Or use Docking Tools - Future versions may support longer sequences
I need maximum accuracy → Use ESMFold2 with MSA - Request on Biohub - 3-5% better accuracy with multiple sequence alignment
I need to screen thousands of structures quickly → Use ESMFold2-Fast - 1.3x faster than ESMFold2 - Minimal accuracy trade-off

title: Decision Tree
text:
2D. Mutation Scoring & Variant Effects

What’s your goal?
Predict effects of all possible mutations (variant effect prediction) → Use ESMC with log-likelihood ratios - Mutation Scoring Tutorial - Variant Prediction Example
Find stabilizing mutations for protein engineering → Use ESMC + ESMFold2 - Score with ESMC - Validate stability with structure - Stability Engineering Example
Understand disease-causing mutations → Use ESMC - Disease Prediction Tutorial - Compare wild-type vs. mutant log-likelihood
Protein function prediction → Use ESMC - Function information in layer 50-60 - Function Prediction Example

title: Model Development
text:
Papers in this section describe the models themselves and methodological advances that enable better representations of protein biology.



Title
Description
Link
Model
Usage




Protein Electrostatic Properties are Fine-Tuned






Through Evolution
The study aims to predict the ionization states (pKa values) of amino acids in proteins directly from sequence alone, using protein language models (pLLMs) instead of requiring 3D structural data.
Link
ESM-C, ESM2, ESM3
Extracted per-residue embeddings from specific transformer layers of ESM2/ESMC models and fed them into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to predict residue-specific pKa values — resulting in KaML-ESM. Sequence → ESM embeddings → MLP → pKa prediction


Training on test proteins improves fitness, structure, and function prediction
This paper proposes a test-time training (TTT) framework for protein machine learning, where a pretrained protein model (e.g., ESM-family) is adapted on the single test protein sequence itself by minimizing its mask-prediction perplexity before downstream inference. This adaptation improves performance on tasks where distribution shift and data scarcity are limiting factors, including protein fitness prediction, structure prediction, and function classification.
Link
ESM-fold, ESM2, ESM3
They take pretrained ESM language models and fine-tune them at test time on the single query protein sequence, using the same self-supervised masked language modeling objective used in pretraining, effectively adapting the model to better represent that specific protein. The adapted model is then used unchanged for downstream predictions — for instance, improving structure prediction via ESMFold+TTT or fitness prediction via ESM-2+TTT, where test-time optimization reduces sequence perplexity and yields better task performance.


Learning millisecond protein dynamics from what is missing in NMR spectra
This paper introduces Dyna-1, a deep learning model trained to predict millisecond-timescale (μs–ms) protein dynamics from missing backbone amide assignments in NMR spectra. The authors curated two major datasets — RelaxDB (133 proteins with experimental NMR relaxation data) and mBMRB (∼9,000 proteins with missing chemical shift assignments) — to train and evaluate their models. The key hypothesis is that missing peaks in NMR data often indicate residues undergoing exchange broadening due to conformational dynamics.
Link
ESM3
The best-performing model, Dyna-1, uses intermediate layer (layer 22) embeddings from ESM-3. These embeddings were critical in enabling the model to learn correlations between sequence/structure features and dynamic behavior. The model was benchmarked against ESM-2, AlphaFold, and other variants, and ESM-3 significantly outperformed others.


AI.zymes – A modular platform for evolutionary enzyme design
AI.zymes is an integrated computational platform for de novo enzyme design. It combines multiple state-of-the-art tools (e.g. Rosetta, ESMFold, ProteinMPNN, etc.) in an iterative evolutionary algorithm to optimize enzyme sequences for improved catalytic properties In a case study, the system engineered variants of a ketosteroid isomerase enzyme, achieving a 7.7-fold increase in a target activity after only one design round.
Link
ESM-fold
The platform incorporates ESMFold to predict protein structures during each design cyclehttps://www.researchgate.net/publication/388302117_AIzymes_-_A_modular_platform_for_evolutionary_enzyme_design#:~:text=engineering%20algorithms%20within%20an%20evolutionary,shot. This allows AI.zymes to evaluate and optimize sequence changes with structural context, drawing on ESM’s learned protein representations for accurate folding predictions.


TIGR-Tas: A family of modular RNA-guided DNA-targeting systems in prokaryotes and their viruses
This paper identifies and characterizes a new family of RNA-guided DNA-targeting systems, called TIGR-Tas, encoded mostly in bacteriophages, archaeal viruses, and parasitic bacteria. These systems utilize a unique tandem-spacer architecture embedded in Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR) arrays that guide associated proteins (Tas) to target DNA sequences. The system features novel combinations of RNA and protein domains, some with nucleases (HNH, RuvC), and demonstrates programmable genome editing, including in human cells.
Link
ESM-fold, ESM2
ESM-2 (15B) was used to generate protein embeddings from the final transformer layer, which informed community detection and clustering of novel Nop domain proteins—crucial to discovering TIGR-Tas systems.


Integrating Protein Language Models and Automatic Biofoundry for Enhanced Protein Evolution
This study describes a biofoundry-integrated pipeline where AI-generated proteins are automatically synthesized, expressed, and tested using robotics. The pipeline was evaluated by evolving enzymes for enhanced catalytic activity using a minimal experimental dataset. The system allows rapid iteration between model generation and experimental testing.
Link
ESM-1v, ESM2
ESM-1v and ESM-2 were used to generate protein sequences with improved function, guided by embeddings and structure-based metrics. These models helped prioritize sequences for lab testing.


Enhancing the Efficiency of Protein Language Models with Minimal Wet-Lab Data through Few-Shot Learning
The authors explored how few-shot learning can adapt large protein language models using minimal wet-lab experimental data. They tested their method (FSFP) across various tasks like fluorescence prediction and solubility, showing generalization from tiny data samples. Their workflow links lab data to rapid reweighting of model representations.
Link
ESM-1v, ESM2
They fine-tuned ESM-1v and ESM-2 on a limited number of experimentally annotated sequences. This reduced the need for large-scale retraining or lab screening.


Predicting Metal-binding Proteins and Structures Through Integration of Evolutionary-scale and Physics-based Modeling
The authors present ESMBind, a two-stage workflow that combines ESM-2 and ESM-IF with physics-based modeling to predict metal-binding residues and generate 3D protein–metal complex structures. The method begins with deep learning–based residue-level predictions, then uses a local grid search and energy minimization to place metal ions realistically within protein structures. ESMBind was tested across seven biologically important metals and applied to predict metal-binding functions in uncharacterized fungal pathogen proteins.
Link
ESM-IF, ESM2
ESMBind integrates two ESM models:



• ESM-2 (650M): used for sequence embeddings, capturing evolutionary-scale sequence information. • ESM-IF: used for structure-aware embeddings, encoding geometric and structural features. These embeddings are fused and fed into a deep learning model that predicts per-residue metal-binding probabilities. This use of ESM models enables accurate, scalable, and generalizable predictions without requiring protein-specific retraining | | DyAb: sequence-based antibody design and property prediction in a low-data regime | DyAb is a deep learning framework for antibody engineering that excels with very limited training data. Built atop a pre-trained protein language model, it predicts changes in antibody binding affinity (and other properties) by modeling pairs of antibody sequences rather than absolute values. In tests on three antibody–antigen systems, DyAb achieved high correlation (Spearman ρ up to 0.85) between predicted and measured affinity changes using as few as ~100 samples. It also generated new antibody sequences via an embedded genetic algorithm, some of which showed >10-fold higher binding affinity than the original leads | Link | ESM2 | DyAb is built on a pre-trained protein language model (one option evaluated was Meta’s ESM-2), which provides rich sequence embeddings. These ESM-derived representations capture evolutionary and biophysical features of antibodies, which DyAb uses to predict affinity changes upon mutation. In essence, ESM’s learned protein context enables DyAb to identify subtle sequence–function relationships and propose beneficial mutations even with limited experimental data. | | Using artificial intelligence to document the hidden RNA virosphere | The study presents LucaProt, a transformer-based deep learning model that integrates protein sequence and structural information to identify highly divergent RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs), which are signature markers of RNA viruses. Using LucaProt on over 10,000 metatranscriptomes from global ecosystems, the team uncovered 161,979 potential RNA virus species and 180 viral supergroups, significantly expanding the known RNA virosphere. | Link | ESM2 | The model incorporates ESM2-3B to extract residue-level structural embeddings of protein sequences. These embeddings are key to the model’s success in identifying highly divergent RdRP domains that traditional tools miss. | | Target sequence-conditioned design of peptide binders using masked language modeling | Presents PepMLM, a deep learning framework that designs de novo peptide binders to arbitrary protein targets solely from sequence, without requiring structural information. It achieves this by finetuning the ESM-2 protein language model to reconstruct masked binder sequences conditioned on target protein sequences, generating peptides that exhibit low perplexity and strong predicted and experimental binding to disease-relevant targets. | Link | ESM2 | PepMLM finetunes ESM-2 with a span masking strategy that places the entire peptide binder region as masked tokens appended to target protein sequences; the model is trained to reconstruct the masked binder conditional on the target. During generation, the target sequence plus mask tokens are fed into the model, which then decodes peptide sequences predicted to bind the target. | | Disease diagnostics using machine learning of B cell and T cell receptor sequences | This study develops MAchine Learning for Immunological Diagnosis (Mal-ID), a framework that uses immune receptor sequencing (BCR and TCR) combined with machine learning and protein language model embeddings to classify disease states from human blood samples. They show that patterns in immune receptor repertoires can accurately distinguish among infections (e.g., SARS-CoV-2, influenza), autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus, type 1 diabetes), and vaccination status with high performance. | Link | ESM2 | The authors computed ESM-2 latent representations for each BCR and TCR sequence and then trained specialized machine learning classifiers (separate for IGHV/isotype groups in BCRs and for TRBV groups in TCRs) to predict disease states from those embeddings. These learned representations captured meaningful structural and immunological features that improved disease classification performance when integrated into the Mal-ID framework. | | De novo design of peptide binders to conformationally diverse targets with contrastive language modeling | This paper presents PepPrCLIP, a purely sequence-based pipeline for de novo design of short peptide binders to protein targets using a combination of protein language model–based generation and CLIP-style contrastive ranking sciadv.adr8638. The authors experimentally validate that PepPrCLIP-designed peptides can bind, inhibit, and induce degradation of structured enzymes (UltraID), transcriptional regulators (β-catenin), and highly disordered fusion oncoproteins (SS18-SSX1) in vitro | Link | ESM2 | They use ESM-2-650M embeddings in two places: (1) to generate naturalistic peptide candidates by applying Gaussian noise to residue-level ESM-2 latent embeddings and decoding them back into amino acid sequences sciadv.adr8638; (2) as frozen input features to a CLIP-style contrastive model, where peptide and target protein sequences are embedded with ESM-2, averaged across sequence length, passed through small MLP encoders, and optimized to maximize cosine similarity for true binding pairs sciadv.adr8638. Importantly, ESM-2 is not fine-tuned; it is used as a frozen pretrained embedding model. | | Engineering of CRISPR-Cas PAM recognition using deep learning of vast evolutionary data | This paper introduces Protein2PAM, a protein language model-based framework for predicting PAM (protospacer-adjacent motif) specificities of CRISPR-Cas systems directly from protein sequences. The model was trained on a massive dataset of over 45,000 PAMs across CRISPR-Cas Types I, II, and V, enabling in silico deep mutational scanning and prediction of PAM-interacting residues without structural information. | Link | ESM2 | The authors used a pretrained ESM-2 protein language model (650M parameters) as the backbone of Protein2PAM. This transformer model encoded the Cas protein sequences and was fine-tuned during training to predict nucleotide distributions at PAM positions. | | Protein codes promote selective subcellular compartmentalization | The authors developed ProtGPS, a model that identifies sequence motifs (“protein codes”) responsible for directing proteins into specific biomolecular condensates. They revealed a hidden code that determines localization to structures like the nucleolus. | Link | ESM2 | ProtGPS leveraged ESM-2 to learn sequence grammar in disordered regions, which was key to identifying these subtle localization codes. The ESM-derived representations enabled pattern discovery that traditional models had missed. | | Learning the language of antibody hypervariability | This paper presents AbMAP, a transfer learning framework that fine-tunes protein language models to specialize in antibody variable regions, especially CDRs. It uses structural and binding data to adapt general models to the antibody domain. | Link | ESM2 | The foundation model used was ESM-2, which was fine-tuned to better represent the highly variable regions of antibodies. ESM’s embeddings helped AbMAP learn nuanced sequence–structure–function relationships in immune proteins. | | Rapid in silico directed evolution by a protein language model with EVOLVEpro | The authors introduce EVOLVEpro, a computational framework that uses a protein language model to guide directed evolution of proteins. It couples ESM-based embeddings with a regression model to iteratively suggest beneficial mutations. | Link | ESM2 | ESM-2 was used to generate sequence embeddings rich in evolutionary context, enabling the model to predict functional mutations across varied protein families. Its output served as the foundation for active learning cycles in EVOLVEpro. | | DiffDock: Diffusion Steps, Twists, and Turns for Molecular Docking | uses ESM2 embeddings as input nodes features to a graph-neural net that generates ligand-binding pose predictions: DiffDock introduces a diffusion generative model for molecular docking that directly samples ligand poses in the protein binding site using the physical degrees of freedom (position, orientation, torsion). It outperforms previous methods in accuracy and speed and demonstrates strong generalization to folded protein structures like those generated by ESMFold. | Link | ESM2 | ESM (specifically ESMFold) was used to generate approximate protein structures (apo-structures) for testing. The DiffDock team evaluated how well their model performs when docking ligands to these predicted structures instead of experimentally derived crystal structures. This showed DiffDock’s robustness to structural imperfections in proteins.Additionally, ESM2 language model embeddings were used as features in the neural network, specifically to embed protein residues with rich, pretrained sequence information. These embeddings were input to the score and confidence models to improve docking predictions. | | Designing Diverse and High-Performance Proteins with a Large Language Model in the Loop | The authors proposed a new closed-loop framework for protein design that combines LLMs with in-the-loop screening to iteratively improve protein candidates. They generated thousands of protein sequences and selected a subset for wet-lab synthesis and testing. Their focus was on achieving high diversity and performance across multiple protein functions. | Link | ESM2 | They used ESM2 to generate and score diverse protein candidates, integrating the model as a backbone for de novo design. ESM predictions were filtered using additional functional constraints before moving to synthesis. | | A General Temperature-Guided Language Model to Design Proteins of Enhanced Stability and Activity | This study presents a novel approach that integrates temperature constraints into the fine-tuning of ESM-2, creating a language model capable of designing proteins with tailored thermal stability. The authors conducted three rounds of mutation, model refinement, and synthesis to create enzyme variants. These were tested in the lab for thermostability and retained biological activity under stress. | Link | ESM2 | ESM-2 was fine-tuned to incorporate temperature sensitivity for stability design. | | FusPB-ESM2: Fusion Model of ProtBERT and ESM-2 for Cell-Penetrating Peptide Prediction | The authors developed a hybrid deep learning framework that combines ESM-2 and ProtBERT for predicting cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs). The model was trained on curated peptide datasets and tested both computationally and experimentally. Top predictions were synthesized and validated via uptake assays in mammalian cells. | Link | ESM2 | ESM-2 was used to extract high-dimensional representations (embeddings) of peptide sequences. These embeddings were fused with ProtBERT’s contextual outputs for robust classification. | | PTM-Mamba: a PTM-aware protein language model with bidirectional gated Mamba blocks | introduces PTM-Mamba, a protein language model that explicitly represents post-translational modifications (PTMs) by adding PTM tokens and modeling sequences with bidirectional Mamba (state-space) blocks fused with pretrained ESM-2 embeddings. The model is designed to encode both wild-type and PTM-annotated sequences and is evaluated on downstream tasks including disease association, druggability prediction, PTM effects on protein–protein interactions, and zero-shot PTM discovery | Link | ESM2 | They pass wild-type amino acid tokens through ESM-2-650M to obtain embeddings, while PTM tokens are mapped to  for the ESM input, and the full PTM-tokenized sequence is processed by PTM-Mamba’s own embedding layer. They then fuse the ESM-2-650M embeddings with PTM-Mamba embeddings using a learned gating mechanism (sigmoid-activated linear gate) to produce the final representation used for training and downstream tasks. | | ESM-Ezy: a deep learning strategy for the mining of novel multicopper oxidases with superior properties | Integrating ESM-1b to discover bioremediation enzymes with improved properties and low sequence similarity. Got some pretty unique structural features and 44% success rate in outperforming query enzymes.The authors developed ESM-Ezy, a fine-tuned ESM-1b model for identifying novel multicopper oxidases (MCOs) with superior catalytic properties using protein embeddings and semantic similarity. Experimental validation confirmed that many predicted enzymes outperform known ones in industrial and environmental applications, showing the power of PLM-guided enzyme discovery. | Link | ESM-1b | The authors used ESM-1b, a pretrained protein language model, and fine-tuned it on a curated set of 147 known multicopper oxidases (MCOs) and over 550,000 non-MCOs. This fine-tuned model, called ESM-Ezy, was used to embed protein sequences into a semantic space. Candidates with short Euclidean distances to known enzymes (query enzymes or QEs) were selected for experimental testing. This approach allowed discovery of functionally similar enzymes with low sequence similarity but high catalytic potential. | | Efficient evolution of human antibodies from general protein language models | Efficiently evolving antibodies with ESM-1b/1v: General protein language models, without any knowledge of target antigen or protein structure, can guide rapid and efficient evolution of human antibodies by suggesting evolutionarily plausible mutations. Lab validation across seven antibodies confirmed substantial improvements in binding affinity, thermostability, and viral neutralization, demonstrating broad utility for therapeutic design | Link | ESM-1b, ESM-1v | The authors used ESM-1b and ESM-1v protein language models to rank single-residue substitutions by how evolutionarily plausible they are (i.e., how likely they are given the training data). They selected top-ranking substitutions that had higher likelihoods than the wild-type across multiple models. These substitutions were then experimentally tested for improved antibody binding affinity. | | Cross-protein transfer learning substantially improves disease variant prediction | Developed CPT-1, a cross-protein transfer learning model trained on DMS data from only five proteins, which integrates ESM-1v, EVE, vertebrate conservation, and structural features. CPT-1 outperforms existing tools on disease variant prediction and enables proteome-wide prediction of all possible missense variants in 90% of human genes. | Link | ESM-1v | Used ESM-1v as a zero-shot predictor of variant effects. ESM-1v’s log-likelihood differences between wild-type and mutant residues were included as features in a supervised model (CPT-1) trained on deep mutational scanning (DMS) data. The authors also extended ESM-1v to handle proteins longer than its default input limit using overlapping windows. |

title: FAQ
text:
Installation & Setup


Q: How do I install the ESM package?
A:
pip install esm
Or for the latest development version:
pip install git+https://github.com/Biohub/esm.git@main
Requirements: - Python 3.10+ - PyTorch 2.0+ - CUDA 11.8+ (for GPU acceleration)
Related: Getting Started | Tutorials



Q: Do I need an API key to use ESM locally?
A: No. You can download ESMC and ESMFold2 from HuggingFace and run them locally without authentication.
You only need an API key if you’re using the Biohub web platform.
Links: HuggingFace Models | Biohub API



Q: What are the hardware requirements?
A: - Embeddings (ESMC): Can run on CPU, but GPU (4GB VRAM) much faster - Structure Prediction (ESMFold2): GPU recommended (16GB+ VRAM for large complexes) - Design: Depends on inference-time search budget
For production use, 24GB VRAM GPU recommended.
Related: Model Comparison

title: FAQ
text:
Usage & Troubleshooting


Q: How do I get embeddings with ESMC?
A: See our Embeddings Tutorial.
Quick code:
import esm

model = esm.pretrained.esmfold_v1()
sequences = ["MKFLK...", "MKVLA..."]
embeddings = model(sequences)
Related: Tutorial | Decision Tree



Q: How long does ESMFold2 take to predict a structure?
A: - Single chain (1024 aa): ~15 seconds (ESMFold2), ~10 seconds (ESMFold2-Fast) on H100 GPU - Complex (2x 300 aa): ~30 seconds - CPU: 10-100x slower
Time scales roughly linearly with sequence length.
Related: Model Comparison | Performance Benchmarks



Q: Can I use ESMFold2 for proteins longer than 2048 residues?
A: ESMFold2 has a 2048 token limit total (all chains combined).
Options: 1. Predict individual chains separately, then dock 2. Use overlapping window approach 3. Request support in Biohub for longer sequences
Related: Known Limitations | Decision Tree



Q: How do I score mutations with ESMC?
A: Use log-likelihood ratio approach:
# Get likelihood for wild-type and mutant
wt_likelihood = model(sequence)["logits"][position, wt_aa]
mut_likelihood = model(mutant_seq)["logits"][position, mut_aa]

# Compute log-likelihood ratio
score = mut_likelihood - wt_likelihood
See our Mutation Scoring Tutorial.
Related: Tutorial | Use Cases

title: FAQ
text:
Design & Predictions


Q: Can I use ESM models to design proteins from scratch?
A: Yes, use ESM3. It generates novel protein sequences conditioned on structure and function properties.
See our Design Tutorial and Design Use Cases.
Related: Decision Tree | Use Cases



Q: How accurate are structure predictions from ESMFold2?
A: - Antibody-antigen: 50-55% DockQ ≥ 0.23 (single sequence), 55%+ with MSA - Protein-protein: 70-76% success rate - Single chains: Very high accuracy (similar to AlphaFold)
Accuracy depends on sequence quality and complexity.
Related: Model Comparison | Benchmarks



Q: How do I predict ligand binding?
A: ESMFold2 supports small molecule ligands as SMILES strings.
See our Ligand Binding Tutorial.
Related: Tutorial | Use Cases

title: FAQ
text:
Fine-tuning & Adaptation


Q: Can I fine-tune ESMC for my specific task?
A: Yes. ESMC fine-tunes well with modest amounts of task-specific data.
Best practices: - Use smaller models (300M or 600M) for faster iteration - Start with a small learning rate - Use parameter-efficient methods (LoRA)
See our Fine-tuning Tutorial.
Related: Tutorial | Use Cases



Q: How much data do I need to fine-tune?
A: It depends on your task: - Simple properties (e.g., solubility): 100-1000 examples - Complex properties (e.g., binding): 1000-10000 examples - Rare tasks: May need more
Start small and scale up based on performance.
Related: Fine-tuning Tutorial

Digital Los Alamos Game
The author built a multi-agent simulation using ESM3 to explore autonomous scientific discovery. Ten AI agents with domain expertise collaborate across hubs like Health and Defense to design proteins for moonshot projects. Using a two-step ESM3 process—sequence generation and structure prediction—they iterate on designs with minimal human input. The system runs in Unity and uses GPT-4o for dialogue and O3-mini for reasoning.
Link
ESM3
They use ESM3 to generate full protein sequences from masked inputs based on Pfam motifs, then predict their structures to assess design quality using pTM confidence scores. If confidence is low, agents update their memory and iterate on the design in a closed-loop process.


EvoCapsid
What if machine learning could engineer a stealth gene delivery vehicle that functions in the body without triggering immunity? The team used ESM3 to redesign viral proteins to look like human proteins for stealth gene delivery, called EvoCapsid. Completed at the Lux Capital Bio X ML Hackathon in October 2024, won ESM3 Creativity Prize.
Link
ESM3
The team used ESM3 and AlphaFold3 to redesign viral proteins to look like human proteins for stealth gene delivery.


https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.11.10.622830v1
I am trying to develop a simulation method that imitates protein fold evolution. The goal is to study how protein folds originate de novo from random sequences and how they evolve. The basic idea is that we introduce mutations in a population of random amino acid sequences (at this stage, usually short sequences 50-70 aa), evaluate the effect of these mutations on protein structure with ESMfold, select a new set of proteins for further evolution, and repeat the cycle.

In silico evolution of globular protein folds from random sequences
Hi Everyone! I am a visiting postdoc at NIH/NCBI in the Evolutionary Genomics Research Group (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/research/groups/koonin/). My background is molecular modeling and biophysics, and I am trying to develop a simulation method that imitates protein fold evolution. The goal is to study how protein folds originate de novo from random sequences and how they evolve. The basic idea is that we introduce mutations in a population of random amino acid sequences (at this stage, usually short sequences 50-70 aa), evaluate the effect of these mutations on protein structure with ESMfold, select a new set of proteins for further evolution, and repeat the cycle. More details in this https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.11.10.622830v1.A peculiar phenomenon is that under selective pressure, random sequences that mutate stochastically evolve into novel folds, often with very high pLDDT and pTM scores. Other interesting things include the extraction of evolutionary information from simulations that can be provided to AlphaFold or the estimation of protein origination time.I hope to talk with you about how reliable the pLDDT and pTM scores can be in this situation and what other approaches can be used to evaluate the predicted structures. For example, we performed MD simulations, which show that not all proteins with high pLDDT are stable, but this method is slow and expensive.Once the work is published, we will want to switch to the ESM-C, and I would appreciate your recommendations and comments.
Link

A 39.8kb flavi-like virus uses a novel strategy for overcoming the RNA virus error threshold
This study reports the discovery of a 39.8kb RNA virus—the longest known flavi-like virus—identified from a Haliclona sponge metatranscriptome. Unlike other large RNA viruses (e.g., Nidovirales), this virus lacks known proofreading exonuclease domains but appears to encode bacterial-like genes involved in nucleic acid metabolism, possibly supporting genome expansion.
Link
ESM-fold
The authors used ESMFold to model portions of the viral polyprotein. These predictions, combined with AlphaFold, helped identify and annotate conserved and novel protein domains, including structural homologs to known viral proteins and unique bacteria-like components.


Revolutionizing Oncology: The Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Antibody Design and Optimization
The paper presents a framework that uses ESM for the de novo design and optimization of therapeutic antibodies. It includes experimental data showing improved antigen-binding affinity and reduced immunogenicity.
Link
ESM-IF, ESM2
Used ESM-2 and ESM-IF1 to design novel antibody variable regions, focusing on the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), which are critical for antigen binding.

De novo design of peptide binders to conformationally diverse targets with contrastive language modeling
Designing binders to target undruggable proteins presents a formidable challenge in drug discovery. In this work, we provide an algorithmic framework to design short, target-binding linear peptides, requiring only the amino acid sequence of the target protein. To do this, we propose a process to generate naturalistic peptide candidates through Gaussian perturbation of the peptidic latent space of the ESM-2 protein language model and subsequently screen these novel sequences for target-selective interaction activity via a contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP)–based contrastive learning architecture. By integrating these generative and discriminative steps, we create a Peptide Prioritization via CLIP (PepPrCLIP) pipeline and validate highly ranked, target-specific peptides experimentally, both as inhibitory peptides and as fusions to E3 ubiquitin ligase domains. PepPrCLIP-derived constructs demonstrate functionally potent binding and degradation of conformationally diverse, disease-driving targets in vitro. In total, PepPrCLIP empowers the modulation of previously inaccessible proteins without reliance on stable and ordered tertiary structures.
Link
ESM2
nan


Discovery of highly active kynureninases for cancer immunotherapy through protein language model 
This study used ESM-1b to identify novel kynureninase enzymes that degrade immunosuppressive metabolites in tumors. The candidates were synthesized and tested in vitro to validate their ability to boost T-cell activation and support immune response against cancer.
Link
ESM-1b
nan


The Virtual Lab: AI Agents Design New SARS-CoV-2 Nanobodies with Experimental Validation
This paper introduces the “Virtual Lab,” a framework where a team of large language model (LLM) agents, guided by a human researcher, collaboratively conducts complex scientific research. The framework is demonstrated on a real-world task: designing new nanobodies that bind to recent SARS-CoV-2 variants using computational tools like ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta.
Link
ESM-1b
ESM-1b was used to compute log-likelihood ratios of point mutations in nanobody sequences, identifying mutations most likely to improve nanobody quality. The LLM agents scripted a full ESM-based mutation ranking pipeline that guided design iterations.


Genome-wide prediction of disease variant effects with a deep protein language model
This study presents a scalable method to predict the effects of all possible missense mutations in the human genome using ESM1b, a 650M-parameter protein language model. The authors created a workflow that overcomes ESM1b’s length limitations, enabling variant effect prediction across ~42,000 human protein isoforms, covering ~450 million potential mutations.
Link
ESM-1b
They used ESM1b to compute log-likelihood ratio (LLR) scores for each missense mutation, quantifying how likely a mutation is given evolutionary sequence patterns. This approach does not require multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and is generalizable to all proteins, including those lacking homology.


Protein language model-guided engineering of an anti-CRISPR protein for precise genome editing in human cells
Used protein language models to guide the engineering of the anti-CRISPR protein AcrIIA4, aiming to improve CRISPR/Cas9 precision. By combining these models with high-throughput screening, they tested ~10,000 variants and identified ones that blocked off-target edits while preserving on-target activity — offering a path to safer gene editing.
Link
ESM-1v
In the paper, ESM-1v was used to identify functionally important regions (hotspots) in the anti-CRISPR protein AcrIIA4. By scoring how likely a given mutation is under the model, the authors pinpointed residues where changes would most likely affect protein function. These predicted hotspots were then targeted for focused mutagenesis, drastically narrowing the search space and guiding the design of a ~10,000-variant library for experimental screening — enabling efficient discovery of variants that improve CRISPR precision.


De novo designed proteins neutralize lethal snake venom toxins
Researchers used deep learning-based protein design to create de novo proteins capable of neutralizing three-finger toxins (3FTxs) — the key lethal components in elapid snake venoms (e.g., cobras, kraits, mambas). These proteins were designed from scratch (i.e., they have no natural analogs), and were engineered to bind tightly to: • Short-chain α-neurotoxins • Long-chain α-neurotoxins • Cytotoxins They achieved this using computational screening and a small number of experimental iterations to identify the most effective designs
Link
ESM-IF
ESM models, specifically the structure-generating ESM-IF1, were used to design de novo proteins that structurally complement and bind tightly to lethal snake venom toxins. The model enabled accurate inverse folding to generate protein sequences with predicted atomic-resolution structures optimized for high-affinity toxin binding.


Enhancing Antibody Language Models with Structural Information
This study used ESM-IF1 to fine-tune antibody sequences. Structural context was integrated to better predict binding properties, and the top sequences were tested for antigen specificity and binding strength in vitro.
Link
ESM-IF
nan


Predicting absolute protein folding stability using generative models
Shows that ESM-IF can accurately predict absolute protein folding stability using the summed likelihood of the native sequence. Without any retraining, the model achieves competitive accuracy on a benchmark of experimentally measured protein stabilities, offering a promising tool for protein design and biophysics.
Link
ESM-IF
The authors used ESM-IF (Inverse Folding model from the ESM family) to predict absolute protein folding stability (ΔG). Specifically, they summed the log-likelihoods assigned by ESM-IF to the wild-type amino acid sequence given a protein structure and found this sum correlates with experimental ΔG values. The approach assumes that likelihood under ESM-IF reflects fitness and stability, and they benchmarked it against other models like ESM-1b, FoldX, and Chroma.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
Looking to see if text and protein models “converge” on the same representation We argue that representations in AI models, particularly deep networks, are converging. First, we survey many examples of convergence in the literature: over time and across multiple domains, the ways by which different neural networks represent data are becoming more aligned. Next, we demonstrate convergence across data modalities: as vision models and language models get larger, they measure distance between datapoints in a more and more alike way.

ESMC is the newest foundation protein language model. It was trained on 2.8 billion protein sequences and produces high-quality representations that capture protein biology from amino acid composition through function.

Machine learning feature extraction
Functional analysis
Representation learning
New research projects

You have 100,000 enzyme sequences and want to predict activity. Use ESMC embeddings as features for your prediction model.
